claims.text: The degree of lattice distortion is the primary factor governing yield strength in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Lattice distortion in these alloys arises from atomic size mismatch.
Lattice distortion influences deformation and failure behavior.
Increasing lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion more effectively.
Greater lattice distortion leads to higher yield strength.
Greater lattice distortion alters ductility relative to alloys with lower distortion.
Substituting an element to increase atomic size mismatch will produce greater lattice distortion.
XRD peak broadening or high-resolution TEM can provide a quantitative measure of lattice distortion.
Local strain fields associated with lattice distortion impede dislocation glide.
Atomic size differences generate significant local lattice strain.
Local lattice strain acts as an obstacle to dislocation motion through a solid-solution-strengthening mechanism.
The proposed strengthening mechanism may shift deformation mode, ductility, or fracture behavior.
The alloy with higher atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion will exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength relative to the baseline.
The alloy with higher lattice distortion may show reduced ductility or a shifted stress-strain response.
The hypothesis should apply to single-phase solid solutions at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures when dislocation-based plasticity dominates.
The hypothesis may be less applicable when diffusion-driven processes, phase transformations, or short-range ordering dominate.
Changes in stacking-fault energy, ordering, and grain size may also contribute to strength and deformation behavior.
The comparison should use similarly processed, nominally single-phase alloys tested at room temperature at a strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1 in air.
Failure to observe a statistically significant yield-strength increase or altered deformation mode in the higher-distortion alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
